response = "Adjudicating a disputed affiliation turns less on how many words two languages share than on what kind of patterning those words exhibit. Regular sound correspondences between two languages are the standard evidence for genetic relationship, and that evidentiary primacy has produced a procedural demand: the comparative method requires reconstruction of a proto-language from the attested daughter languages. Because that reconstructive demand governs the discipline, mass lexical comparison without reconstruction is rejected by most historical linguists. A procedure that predicts the phonological shape of each cognate form, rather than one that tabulates resemblances, is what makes inheritance and borrowing distinguishable in the first place. Within that framework the available evidence is ranked. Shared irregular morphology is treated as among the strongest evidence of common descent, since suppletive paradigms and arbitrary allomorphy are not transferred wholesale across a contact boundary. By contrast, shared basic word order is accepted by historical linguists as proof of genetic relationship. Typological traits such as tone and monosyllabicity can spread between unrelated neighbouring languages, and that diffusibility cannot be squared with granting shared basic word order the status of proof of common descent. Loanwords cluster in semantic fields tied to trade, religion, and technology, and that distribution confirms that shared basic vocabulary such as body-part and kinship terms is relatively resistant to borrowing. Numerals form a contrast to that merely relative resistance: they are never borrowed between languages in contact. Correspondences concentrated in the resistant core of the lexicon therefore carry a weight that parallels in cultural vocabulary do not. The history of Vietnamese shows how such a dispute is resolved in practice. Henri Maspero classified Vietnamese as a Tai language in 1912, pointing to its tonal system, its monosyllabic word shapes and a sizeable stock of words shared with Tai. At least one of two ordinary explanations covers that shared stock, and perhaps both do: some of the lexical resemblances between Vietnamese and Tai languages are the product of borrowing, these being the very similarities that led Maspero to his classification, and some of the lexical resemblances between Vietnamese and Tai languages are the product of accidental similarity. Once the borrowed layer is set aside, regular correspondences in body-part terms, kinship terms and verbal morphology align Vietnamese with Mon-Khmer, and the borrowed character of the Tai parallels indicates that Vietnamese is a member of the Austroasiatic family. The question admits only two mutually exclusive answers: either Vietnamese belongs to Austroasiatic, or Vietnamese lies outside the Austroasiatic family, one of the two holding and both together being impossible. The reconstruction of Proto-Vietic, with Vietnamese tone emerging from the loss of final laryngeals and initial voicing distinctions, decides which of the two obtains."
